## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Odhisokathā* (Kv 1.4) is the fourth discourse in the first chapter of the *Kathāvatthu*, situated in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. The controversy examined in this text concerns whether defilements (*kilesa*) are abandoned piecemeal or segment by segment (*odhiso odhiso*, *ekadesena ekadesena*) [Bareau 1955]. Opponents maintain that stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and other noble disciples abandon defilements progressively, one part after another, through distinct clear realizations (*nānābhisamayavasena*) when seeing the Noble Truth of suffering and the subsequent truths [Bareau 1955]. Against this, the Theravādin position argues that defilements are not put away piece by piece (*odhiso*); if corruptions were removed incrementally, a practitioner could be partly endowed with one of the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*), which conflicts with the teachings of the Buddha [Aung & Rhys Davids 1915; Bareau 1955].
SuttaCentral records cross-tradition connections and shared passages between Kv 1.4 and several texts, including the *Ratana Sutta* (Snp 2.1), the *Saradasutta* (AN 3.94), other Kathāvatthu debates such as the *Anupubbābhisamayakathā* (Kv 2.9) and *Aññāṇakathā* (Kv 2.2), as well as verses in the Dhammapada and Udānavarga corpora (such as Dhp 239, Patna Dharmapada 157–173, Udānavarga 2, Gāndhārī Dharmapada 61–70, and Chinese translations T 210, T 212, and T 213) [SuttaCentral]. In agreement with SuttaCentral's cross-reference to Kv 2.9, DharmaNexus detects extensive internal text reuse across 83 Pali works, led by Kv 2.9 (290 matches comprising over 41,000 characters) and other related Kathāvatthu discussions such as *Vimuccamānakathā* (Kv 3.4), *Asekhañāṇakathā* (Kv 5.2), and *Parihānikathā* (Kv 1.2), alongside canonical sutta formulas in the *Sotāpatti Saṁyutta* (SN 55) and the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of the text with Sanskrit and Tibetan scholastic treatises, including Asaṅga's *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Śrāvakabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, and Vimalamitra's *Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti* [DharmaNexus].
